rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Judicial Department - judicial power, judicial review, and constitutional supremacy
rows.case_title: Jose A. Angara v. The Electoral Commission, et al.
rows.facts_digest: After Angara was proclaimed elected to the National Assembly, his opponent lodged an election protest before the constitutionally created Electoral Commission. Angara sought prohibition, arguing that an Assembly resolution had already fixed the deadline for protests and foreclosed the Commission's action.
rows.issue: Whether the Electoral Commission had constitutional authority to hear the protest and whether the Supreme Court could determine the boundary between the Commission and the National Assembly.
rows.ruling: The Court held that the Electoral Commission was an independent constitutional tribunal with exclusive authority over contests involving the election, returns, and qualifications of Assembly members. Judicial review remained available to keep constitutional organs within their allotted spheres, but the Commission had not exceeded its authority.
rows.controlling_doctrine: The Constitution is supreme and allocates limited powers among coordinate departments; when constitutional boundaries are disputed, courts may determine the proper allocation without assuming the functions of the other organ.
rows.disposition: Petition for prohibition dismissed; the Electoral Commission could proceed with the election contest.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the classic starting point for judicial review, separation of powers, constitutional supremacy, and the nature of independent constitutional bodies.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: State the constitutional allocation of power, explain that judicial review polices jurisdictional boundaries, apply the specific constitutional grant to the challenged body, then conclude whether grave abuse or usurpation exists.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Executive Department - executive power and residual presidential powers
rows.case_title: Ferdinand E. Marcos, et al. v. Hon. Raul Manglapus, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Former President Ferdinand Marcos and his family, then in exile, sought to return to the Philippines. President Corazon Aquino refused because of assessed threats to national security, political stability, and public order, prompting a petition to compel their return.
rows.issue: Whether the President could bar the Marcos family's return despite the absence of an express constitutional power specifically addressing that exceptional situation.
rows.ruling: The Court sustained the President's decision as an exercise of residual executive power and her duty to protect the nation. It distinguished the right to return to one's country from the constitutionally qualified liberty of travel and treated the controversy as exceptional and fact-specific.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Executive power is not confined to powers itemized in the Constitution; the President retains residual authority necessary to discharge the office, subject to the Constitution, statute, and judicial review for grave abuse.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed; the presidential decision temporarily barring return was sustained.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It anchors questions on the scope of executive power, national security, the right to travel, and review of presidential fact-finding.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the claimed right and the source of executive authority, distinguish express from residual powers, test necessity and constitutional limits, and emphasize the extraordinary factual setting before concluding.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: State policies and environmental rights - intergenerational responsibility and standing
rows.case_title: Juan Antonio Oposa, et al. v. Hon. Fulgencio S. Factoran, Jr., et al.
rows.facts_digest: Minors, represented by their parents, sued to cancel existing timber license agreements and prevent further depletion of Philippine rainforests. The trial court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a cause of action and on political-question grounds.
rows.issue: Whether the minors had standing, including for generations yet unborn, and stated an enforceable claim based on the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology.
rows.ruling: The Court recognized the minors' standing for themselves and succeeding generations and held that the complaint stated a cause of action. The environmental right and the corresponding State duty were enforceable, while the case required factual proceedings rather than dismissal at the pleading stage.
rows.controlling_doctrine: The right to a balanced and healthful ecology carries an intergenerational responsibility; representatives of the present generation may sue to prevent serious impairment of resources held for present and future Filipinos.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; the dismissal orders were set aside and the civil case was allowed to proceed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the principal Philippine authority on environmental constitutionalism, standing, intergenerational justice, and causes of action grounded in Article II.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Connect the environmental harm to the constitutional right and statutory duties, establish representative standing and threatened injury, then explain why judicial relief is justiciable.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: National Economy and Patrimony - Regalian doctrine, reclaimed lands, and right to information
rows.case_title: Francisco I. Chavez v. Public Estates Authority and Amari Coastal Bay Development Corporation
rows.facts_digest: The Public Estates Authority negotiated an amended joint venture under which Amari, a private corporation, would acquire large areas of reclaimed and still-to-be-reclaimed Manila Bay lands. Chavez sought disclosure of the negotiations and challenged the transfer.
rows.issue: Whether the amended joint venture could lawfully convey reclaimed public-domain lands to a private corporation and whether negotiation records were covered by the constitutional right to information.
rows.ruling: The Court held that the reclaimed lands remained lands of the public domain while held by the government and could not be transferred to a private corporation contrary to Article XII. It also enforced public access to information on the government transaction.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Under the Regalian doctrine, lands not shown to have become alienable patrimonial property remain with the State; private corporations may lease but generally may not acquire alienable lands of the public domain, and transactions of public concern are subject to constitutional transparency.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; PEA and Amari were permanently enjoined and the amended joint venture was declared void ab initio.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It integrates land classification, constitutional nationality restrictions, standing, mandamus, and the right to information in one frequently tested authority.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Classify the land at each stage, identify the transferee's constitutional qualification, apply the public-domain prohibition, and separately analyze access to official negotiation records.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Bill of Rights - search warrants, particularity, probable cause, and exclusionary rule
rows.case_title: Harry S. Stonehill, et al. v. Hon. Jose W. Diokno, et al.
rows.gr_number: G.R. No. L-19550 and companion cases
rows.facts_digest: Dozens of warrants authorized sweeping searches of residences and corporate offices for evidence of broadly stated violations of several bodies of law. The applications did not identify a specific offense or particularly describe the items to be seized.
rows.issue: Whether the warrants were unconstitutional general warrants and whether the individual petitioners could suppress materials seized from both their homes and corporate premises.
rows.ruling: The Court declared the residence warrants void for lack of a specific offense, probable-cause particularity, and a particular description of things to be seized. It adopted the exclusionary rule but limited relief by standing, distinguishing personal effects from corporate records or premises not shown to be under the individuals' exclusive control.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A warrant must rest on probable cause for one specific offense and particularly describe the place and things; evidence obtained through an unconstitutional search is inadmissible, but suppression ordinarily requires invasion of the claimant's own protected interest.
rows.disposition: Relief granted for personal effects seized from the petitioners' residences; relief denied as to materials seized from other offices and corporate premises for lack of standing.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the foundational Philippine authority on general warrants, particularity, exclusion, and personal standing in search-and-seizure litigation.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Test the warrant for a specific offense, judicially determined probable cause, and particularity; then separately ask whether the accused may invoke exclusion for the place or property searched.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Accountability of Public Officers - impeachment and the one-year bar
rows.case_title: Ernesto B. Francisco, Jr., et al. v. House of Representatives, et al.
rows.facts_digest: After an earlier impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Hilario Davide, Jr. had been filed and referred, legislators filed a second complaint within one year. Petitions challenged the House rules and the second complaint under Article XI, Section 3(5).
rows.issue: Whether the controversy was judicially reviewable and when an impeachment proceeding is initiated for purposes of the constitutional one-year bar.
rows.ruling: The Court exercised expanded judicial review and held that initiation occurs upon filing and referral of the complaint to the proper House committee. The second complaint fell within the one-year prohibition, and inconsistent House rules were unconstitutional.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Impeachment is political but not beyond judicial review when a constitutional limitation is alleged; the one-year bar is triggered by filing and referral of the first complaint.
rows.disposition: Relevant House impeachment rules declared unconstitutional and the second complaint barred.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the controlling framework for impeachment initiation, justiciability, political questions, and expanded judicial power.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the textual impeachment limit, establish the legally operative event of initiation, apply the one-year period, and address judicial review through grave-abuse jurisdiction.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Executive Department - commander-in-chief powers, national emergency, and emergency takeover
rows.case_title: Prof. Randolf S. David, et al. v. Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Following alleged coup threats and public demonstrations, the President issued Proclamation No. 1017 declaring a national emergency and General Order No. 5. Authorities conducted warrantless arrests, dispersed rallies, and searched a newspaper office.
rows.issue: Which portions of the emergency proclamation and implementing acts were within presidential power, and which required legislation or violated protected rights.
rows.ruling: The Court upheld the call-out power to suppress lawless violence and the declaration of a state of emergency, but invalidated commands to enforce unrelated laws or presidential decrees, any takeover of private utilities without enabling legislation, and unlawful arrests, dispersals, and searches.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A declaration of emergency does not itself enlarge presidential power; call-out authority is distinct from emergency powers delegated by Congress and from the statutory conditions for takeover of public utilities.
rows.disposition: Petitions partly granted; the proclamation and order were sustained only within constitutional limits, and specified enforcement acts and clauses were invalidated.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It supplies the standard distinctions among call-out power, martial law, suspension of the writ, delegated emergency power, and economic takeover authority.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Classify the presidential act, identify whether congressional delegation is required, test the implementing measure against the Bill of Rights, and sever valid call-out action from invalid excesses.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional change - amendment, revision, and people's initiative
rows.case_title: Raul L. Lambino, et al. v. Commission on Elections, with consolidated case
rows.facts_digest: Proponents gathered signatures for an initiative that would replace the bicameral presidential system with a unicameral parliamentary government. The signature sheets did not contain the full proposed constitutional text, and the proposal comprehensively altered governmental structure.
rows.issue: Whether the petition was directly proposed by the people and constituted an amendment permissible through initiative rather than a revision.
rows.ruling: The Court held that the signatories were not shown the full text as constitutionally required and that the sweeping change in the structure and checks of government was a revision beyond the initiative power.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A people's initiative must directly propose the complete amendment to informed signatories; initiative may amend but cannot revise the Constitution, assessed through both quantitative and qualitative change.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed and COMELEC action declining the initiative sustained.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the leading authority on the amendment-revision distinction and the full-text/direct-proposal requirements for constitutional initiative.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Examine what signatories actually saw, classify the proposal by the extent and nature of institutional change, and match the chosen mode to the Constitution's authorized methods.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Public International Law - treaties, executive agreements, and the Visiting Forces Agreement
rows.case_title: Bayan, et al. v. Executive Secretary Ronaldo Zamora, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Petitioners challenged the Visiting Forces Agreement between the Philippines and the United States, including its ratification, its treatment by the United States, and provisions governing visiting U.S. personnel.
rows.issue: Whether the VFA satisfied the constitutional requirements for treaties and whether it was recognized as a treaty by the other contracting state.
rows.ruling: The Court sustained the VFA after Philippine Senate concurrence. It held that U.S. recognition through its constitutional processes was sufficient for the treaty-recognition requirement, even if the United States used a different domestic label.
rows.controlling_doctrine: For an international agreement covered by Article XVIII, Section 25, Philippine Senate concurrence and recognition by the other state as a treaty through its own constitutional processes satisfy the Constitution.
rows.disposition: Consolidated petitions dismissed; the VFA was sustained.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is central to treaty-making, executive agreements, foreign military presence, state consent, and the domestic effect of international agreements.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the constitutional treaty clause implicated, trace ratification and Senate concurrence, evaluate the other state's recognition, and distinguish international validity from domestic nomenclature.

rows.subject: Political and Public International Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Territory and Law of the Sea - archipelagic baselines and regime of islands
rows.case_title: Prof. Merlin M. Magallona, et al. v. Hon. Eduardo Ermita, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Petitioners attacked Republic Act No. 9522, which adjusted Philippine archipelagic baselines to conform with UNCLOS and treated the Kalayaan Island Group and Scarborough Shoal under the regime of islands.
rows.issue: Whether the revised baselines unconstitutionally reduced Philippine territory or sovereignty and whether the treatment of outlying features was valid under UNCLOS.
rows.ruling: The Court upheld the statute, explaining that baselines measure maritime zones rather than define or surrender land territory. Treating outlying features under the regime of islands preserved claims while conforming the baseline system to UNCLOS.
rows.controlling_doctrine: UNCLOS baseline rules delimit maritime entitlements; they do not determine acquisition or loss of land territory, and statutory conformity with those rules does not itself relinquish sovereignty claims.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed; Republic Act No. 9522 declared constitutional.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the principal local case for archipelagic baselines, UNCLOS, territorial claims, internal waters, and maritime zones.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Separate title to land territory from measurement of maritime zones, identify the applicable UNCLOS regime, and explain the legal effect of the baseline classification.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Corporation Law - nationality restrictions and capital in public utilities
rows.case_title: Wilson P. Gamboa v. Finance Secretary Margarito B. Teves, et al.
rows.facts_digest: A PLDT stockholder challenged the government's sale of PTIC shares to a foreign-affiliated buyer, arguing that foreign beneficial ownership and voting control in PLDT exceeded the constitutional limit for public utilities.
rows.issue: What 'capital' means under Article XII, Section 11 and how Filipino ownership and control of a public utility should be measured.
rows.ruling: The Court treated the action as mandamus and held that the constitutional Filipino-ownership requirement protects both effective voting control and beneficial ownership. It directed the SEC to determine and enforce PLDT's compliance.
rows.controlling_doctrine: For constitutionally nationalized public utilities, at least sixty percent of the relevant voting capital and the corresponding beneficial ownership must remain Filipino; formal title cannot be used to defeat effective Filipino control.
rows.disposition: Petition partly granted; the SEC was directed to investigate the ownership structure and impose sanctions if constitutional compliance was lacking.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the anchor for public-utility nationality, beneficial ownership, voting control, and constitutional limits on foreign equity.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the nationalized activity, compute voting and beneficial ownership by class, test actual control rather than labels, and note later clarifications and implementing SEC rules.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Corporation Law and Mining - control test and grandfather rule
rows.case_title: Narra Nickel Mining and Development Corp., et al. v. Redmont Consolidated Mines Corp.
rows.facts_digest: Competing mining applicants disputed whether three applicant corporations were Philippine nationals qualified to exploit natural resources. Their nominal Filipino corporate ownership traced through layers that were substantially funded and controlled by a foreign mining company.
rows.issue: Whether the control test alone established Philippine nationality or whether the grandfather rule should trace actual equity when nationality was doubtful.
rows.ruling: The Court upheld the finding that the applicants were not qualified Philippine nationals. Because the ownership arrangements created genuine doubt and foreign control, equity had to be traced through the corporate layers rather than accepted at face value.
rows.controlling_doctrine: The control test is the initial nationality measure, but the grandfather rule applies when the required Filipino ownership is merely nominal, simulated, or otherwise doubtful, allowing tracing of ultimate ownership and control.
rows.disposition: Petition denied; the Court of Appeals decision disqualifying the mining applicants was affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the key case for layered corporate nationality, anti-dummy concerns, beneficial ownership, and natural-resource exploitation.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Apply the statutory control test first, identify facts creating doubt, trace equity to ultimate owners under the grandfather rule, and conclude whether the corporation is a Philippine national.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Corporation Law - separate juridical personality and piercing the corporate veil
rows.case_title: Concept Builders, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Employees won an illegal-dismissal judgment against Concept Builders, but execution was frustrated when assets at the same business premises were claimed by a sister corporation with substantially identical ownership and management.
rows.issue: Whether the sister corporation's separate personality could shield assets from execution of the labor judgment.
rows.ruling: The Court pierced the corporate veil because the related entity was used as an alter ego and a device to evade a lawful obligation. Corporate fiction could not be invoked to perpetrate fraud or defeat public convenience and justice.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Separate personality may be disregarded when a corporation is a mere instrumentality or alter ego, or when the fiction is used to evade an obligation, justify a wrong, protect fraud, or defeat public convenience.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed; NLRC execution orders reaching property at the sister company's premises were affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It supplies the standard language and factual markers for veil-piercing and alter-ego problems.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Begin with separate personality, identify unity of ownership/control and misuse of the entity, connect that misuse causally to the avoided obligation, and justify exceptional veil-piercing.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Securities Regulation - material nonpublic information and insider trading
rows.case_title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Interport Resources Corporation, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Interport's board approved a major acquisition involving a power-generating company. Before the transaction was publicly disclosed, directors and related persons traded Interport shares, leading to an SEC insider-trading investigation that respondents sought to enjoin.
rows.issue: Whether the SEC could investigate and prosecute trades made while insiders possessed material information not yet disclosed to the public.
rows.ruling: The Court sustained the SEC's authority and the operative prohibition against insider trading. Persons connected with an issuer who possess material nonpublic information must disclose it before trading or abstain from trading.
rows.controlling_doctrine: An insider who possesses material information unavailable to the investing public is subject to the disclose-or-abstain rule; materiality turns on whether a reasonable investor would consider the information important.
rows.disposition: The respondents' attempt to stop the SEC proceeding failed; the SEC could continue its action.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the leading local decision explaining insider status, materiality, disclosure, and securities-regulator authority.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the trader's relationship to the issuer, determine whether the information was material and nonpublic, apply disclose-or-abstain, and address SEC investigative jurisdiction.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Intellectual Property - trademark infringement and unfair competition
rows.case_title: McDonald's Corporation and McGeorge Food Industries, Inc. v. L.C. Big Mak Burger, Inc., et al.
rows.short_title: McDonald's v. L.C. Big Mak Burger
rows.facts_digest: McDonald's, owner of the registered BIG MAC mark and related trade dress, sued a local hamburger business using BIG MAK and presentation features that allegedly caused consumer confusion.
rows.issue: Whether BIG MAK infringed the registered BIG MAC mark and constituted unfair competition despite differences in spelling and business presentation.
rows.ruling: The Court found confusing similarity using the dominancy test and held the defendants liable for trademark infringement and unfair competition. The dominant aural and visual features, related goods, and manner of sale were likely to mislead ordinary purchasers.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Trademark infringement focuses on likelihood of confusion, with the dominancy test giving weight to prevalent features rather than requiring exact copying; unfair competition additionally examines deceptive passing off and overall presentation.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; the Court of Appeals was set aside and the trial court judgment finding infringement and unfair competition was reinstated.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard Philippine case for the dominancy test, likelihood of confusion, and the distinction between infringement and unfair competition.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Compare dominant mark features, goods, channels, purchasers, and presentation; separately apply registered-mark infringement and passing-off elements.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Negotiable Instruments and Credit Transactions - bearer instruments and pledge of incorporeal rights
rows.case_title: Caltex (Philippines), Inc. v. Court of Appeals and Security Bank and Trust Company
rows.facts_digest: A depositor delivered bearer certificates of time deposit to Caltex as security for fuel purchases, then reported them lost and executed a notarized assignment to the issuing bank for his loan. Caltex later demanded the proceeds.
rows.issue: Whether the certificates were negotiable and whether their delivery as collateral gave Caltex a right enforceable against the bank's documented assignment.
rows.ruling: The certificates were negotiable bearer instruments, but the transaction was a pledge rather than an outright negotiation. Without the required indorsement and a public instrument making the pledge effective against third persons, Caltex had no superior right over the bank.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Negotiability of the instrument does not dispense with Civil Code requirements governing a pledge of incorporeal rights; the legal effect depends on whether delivery transfers title or merely creates collateral security.
rows.disposition: Petition denied and the judgment for the bank affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It forces examinees to distinguish negotiability, negotiation, holder status, assignment, and pledge requirements.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Determine negotiability from the face, characterize the transfer's true purpose, apply the correct mode of negotiation or pledge formalities, then rank competing claims.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Insurance - concealment, materiality, and interpretation of insurance applications
rows.case_title: Great Pacific Life Assurance Corp. v. Court of Appeals and Medarda V. Leuterio
rows.short_title: Great Pacific Life v. Court of Appeals
rows.facts_digest: A physician insured under a DBP group mortgage-life policy died, and the insurer refused payment by alleging that he had concealed hypertension and a heart condition in his application.
rows.issue: Whether the insured made a material concealment that entitled the insurer to avoid the policy.
rows.ruling: The Court found no proven fraudulent or material concealment and construed ambiguities against the insurer that drafted the application. The insurer remained liable for the policy proceeds.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Concealment requires failure to communicate a material fact known to the insured; the insurer bears the consequences of ambiguous questions and must prove the factual basis for avoidance.
rows.disposition: Petition denied; payment of the insurance proceeds to the insured's heirs, subject to prior settlement of the mortgage debt, was ordered.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is an accessible anchor for concealment, materiality, burden of proof, and contra proferentem in insurance contracts.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the allegedly withheld fact, knowledge, materiality to the risk, and the wording of the application; then assess whether avoidance was timely and proven.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Transportation Law - common carriers, vessel collision, and COGSA limitation
rows.case_title: National Development Company v. Court of Appeals and Development Insurance & Surety Corporation, with companion case
rows.short_title: National Development Co. v. Court of Appeals
rows.facts_digest: Cargo aboard the M/V Dona Nati was lost or damaged after a collision with another vessel. The vessel owner and charterer resisted liability and invoked carriage-law defenses and limitation provisions.
rows.issue: Whether the vessel owner and charterer were liable as common carriers and whether the cargo claim was timely under COGSA.
rows.ruling: The Court treated the responsible shipping parties as common carriers answerable for the cargo loss and upheld the timely claim. They could not avoid the extraordinary-diligence obligations attached to the carriage undertaking.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A vessel owner and a charterer that actually undertake public carriage may both bear common-carrier obligations; cargo claims must also be tested against the one-year COGSA period measured from delivery or when delivery should have occurred.
rows.disposition: Petitions denied and the appellate judgment imposing liability affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It combines common-carrier status, solidary liability, collision, extraordinary diligence, and COGSA prescription.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Classify each shipping party's operational role, apply extraordinary diligence and presumptions for lost cargo, then calculate the COGSA filing period.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Taxation - lifeblood doctrine, due process, and ordinary business deductions
rows.case_title: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Algue, Inc. and Court of Tax Appeals
rows.facts_digest: The BIR disallowed Algue's deduction of professional and promotional fees paid for work that enabled the company to obtain a lucrative transaction, then assessed deficiency income tax. Algue protested and challenged the assessment.
rows.issue: Whether the fees were legitimate deductible business expenses and whether tax collection could disregard procedural fairness.
rows.ruling: The Court found the payments reasonable, ordinary, and necessary in light of the services rendered, and sustained the deduction. Although taxes are the lifeblood of government, collection must remain authorized by law and consistent with due process.
rows.controlling_doctrine: The lifeblood doctrine does not license arbitrary taxation; a taxpayer may deduct substantiated ordinary and necessary business expenses that are reasonable and connected with the trade or business.
rows.disposition: Court of Tax Appeals decision favoring Algue affirmed in full.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the canonical opening authority for balancing efficient tax collection with legality, fairness, and deductible-business-expense rules.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Acknowledge the State's taxing power, identify the statutory deduction, prove business connection and reasonableness, and test assessment procedure before concluding liability.

rows.subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
rows.syllabus_topic: Tax Remedies - VAT refund administrative waiting and judicial appeal periods
rows.case_title: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. San Roque Power Corporation, with Taganito Mining Corporation and Philex Mining Corporation cases
rows.facts_digest: Three taxpayers sought judicial refunds of unutilized input VAT at different points relative to the statutory administrative waiting period, the appeal period, and BIR Ruling No. DA-489-03.
rows.issue: Whether compliance with the administrative waiting period and the subsequent period for appeal to the CTA was mandatory, and when taxpayers could rely on the contrary BIR ruling.
rows.ruling: The Court treated the statutory sequence as mandatory and resolved the three claims according to their filing dates. It recognized a limited period when good-faith reliance on BIR Ruling No. DA-489-03 excused premature judicial filing.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A tax-refund claimant must follow the statutory administrative and judicial periods then in force; an official BIR interpretation may create a narrow non-retroactivity or equitable-reliance exception until judicially reversed.
rows.disposition: The consolidated cases were resolved differently according to timeliness and the applicable reliance window; San Roque and Philex were denied relief while Taganito obtained the benefit of the BIR-ruling exception.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the anchor for CTA jurisdiction, VAT-refund timing, administrative exhaustion, and non-retroactivity of adverse changes in tax interpretation.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Build a dated timeline, apply the version of the NIRC governing the claim, compute each mandatory period, and test whether an official-ruling reliance exception applies.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Persons and Family Relations - psychological incapacity under Article 36
rows.case_title: Rosanna L. Tan-Andal v. Mario Victor M. Andal
rows.facts_digest: Rosanna sought nullity of her marriage, presenting evidence of Mario's enduring pattern of irresponsibility, drug use, financial dependence, absence, and failure to perform essential marital obligations. The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decree of nullity under the restrictive Molina framework.
rows.issue: How psychological incapacity under Article 36 should be proved and whether Mario's demonstrated personality structure met the legal standard.
rows.ruling: The Court restored the decree of nullity and reformulated Article 36 doctrine. Psychological incapacity is a legal, not medical, concept; expert diagnosis is not indispensable, and clear and convincing evidence may establish a grave, enduring, and legally antecedent incapacity manifested through consistent acts.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Psychological incapacity is an enduring aspect of personality structure that makes a spouse genuinely unable, not merely unwilling, to perform essential marital obligations; juridical antecedence, gravity, and incurability are legal concepts proved by the totality of evidence.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; the Court of Appeals was reversed and the trial court decision declaring the marriage void was reinstated.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the present anchor for Article 36 and expressly recalibrates the older Molina guidelines.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: State Tan-Andal's legal standard, distinguish inability from refusal or ordinary marital difficulty, organize facts showing antecedence, gravity, and endurance, then assess the clear-and-convincing-evidence threshold.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Persons and Family Relations - recognition of foreign divorce under Article 26
rows.case_title: Republic of the Philippines v. Marelyn Tanedo Manalo
rows.facts_digest: A Filipino woman married a Japanese national in the Philippines and later obtained a divorce decree in Japan. She petitioned to cancel the marriage entry, while the Republic argued that Article 26 did not benefit a Filipino spouse who initiated the foreign divorce.
rows.issue: Whether Article 26 may capacitate the Filipino spouse to remarry when the valid foreign divorce was initiated by that Filipino spouse.
rows.ruling: The Court held that the provision's remedial purpose prevents the anomalous situation where the foreign spouse is free to remarry but the Filipino remains bound, regardless of who initiated the divorce. The foreign decree and applicable foreign law still had to be alleged and proved as facts.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A valid foreign divorce obtained by the alien spouse or through proceedings initiated by the Filipino spouse may be recognized under Article 26 if it capacitated the alien spouse to remarry; the decree and foreign law require competent proof.
rows.disposition: Republic's petition denied in part; the Article 26 interpretation was sustained and the case remanded for proof of Japanese divorce law.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It governs mixed-marriage foreign-divorce problems, proof of foreign law, civil-registry relief, and capacity to remarry.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Fix each spouse's citizenship at the relevant time, establish a valid foreign divorce and its effect under foreign law, then apply Article 26 and specify the evidentiary proof required.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Property Relations Between Spouses - liquidation after a void marriage
rows.case_title: Antonio A.S. Valdez v. Regional Trial Court, Branch 102, Quezon City, and Consuelo M. Gomez-Valdez
rows.facts_digest: After a marriage was declared void for psychological incapacity, the parties disputed the disposition of their family dwelling and other properties. One spouse argued that ordinary conjugal-partnership rules should govern liquidation.
rows.issue: Which property regime applies when a marriage is void ab initio and how property acquired during cohabitation should be liquidated.
rows.ruling: The Court held that a void marriage produces no valid conjugal partnership. Property relations are governed by the special co-ownership rules in Articles 147 or 148, depending on the parties' legal capacity and circumstances.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Property acquired during a void union is liquidated under the Family Code's co-ownership provisions, not the property regime applicable to a valid marriage.
rows.disposition: Trial court orders applying the proper co-ownership framework were affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the basic authority for distinguishing Articles 147 and 148 from absolute community or conjugal partnership after nullity.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: First determine why the marriage is void and whether the parties were capacitated to marry each other, then choose Article 147 or 148, trace contributions, and allocate the property.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Land Registration - R.A. No. 11573, possession period, and proof of alienability
rows.case_title: Republic of the Philippines v. Pasig Rizal Co., Inc.
rows.facts_digest: Pasig Rizal sought original registration based on long possession, but the Republic challenged the proof that the property had been classified as alienable and disposable. While the case was pending, Republic Act No. 11573 changed the possession and proof requirements.
rows.issue: Whether R.A. No. 11573 applies to pending registration cases and what evidence now proves possession and alienable-and-disposable classification.
rows.ruling: The Court treated the statute as curative and applicable to cases pending when it took effect. Twenty years of qualifying possession immediately before filing may suffice, and Section 7 prescribes the DENR geodetic-engineer certification and authentication framework for land classification.
rows.controlling_doctrine: R.A. No. 11573 retroactively governs pending judicial-confirmation applications as a curative law, subject to its twenty-year possession rule and prescribed competent proof that the land is alienable and disposable.
rows.disposition: Petition denied in part; the possession finding was retained and the case remanded for reception of classification evidence under R.A. No. 11573.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the current En Banc anchor connecting the amended Public Land Act and Property Registration Decree to evidentiary requirements.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Check the filing and pendency dates, apply the twenty-year rule, identify the classification issuance and map, and require the statutory DENR certification and authentication.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Succession - preterition and institution of heirs
rows.case_title: Remedios Nuguid v. Felix Nuguid and Paz Salonga Nuguid
rows.facts_digest: A single decedent's holographic will instituted one sibling as universal heir but completely omitted her surviving legitimate parents, who were compulsory heirs in the direct ascending line. The will contained no other testamentary disposition.
rows.issue: Whether the omission constituted preterition and what effect it had on the sole institution of heir and the will as a whole.
rows.ruling: The Court found total preterition of compulsory heirs in the direct line. Because the sole testamentary provision was the institution of the universal heir, that institution was annulled and intestacy followed.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Preterition is the total omission of a compulsory heir in the direct line from the inheritance without valid disinheritance; it annuls the institution of heir, while independently valid devises and legacies may survive.
rows.disposition: Order treating the will as a complete nullity and dismissing the probate petition affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the canonical preterition case and clarifies the difference among preterition, defective disinheritance, and reduction of inofficious dispositions.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the compulsory heir and direct line, determine whether there was total omission and no valid disinheritance, then state precisely which testamentary provisions are annulled and whether intestacy results.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Sales - perfected contract of sale versus contract to sell
rows.case_title: Romulo A. Coronel, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Sellers accepted a down payment for a house and lot and agreed to transfer title after obtaining it from a financing institution. They later sold the property to another buyer and characterized the first agreement as merely a contract to sell.
rows.issue: Whether the receipt and agreement perfected a contract of sale or only a contract to sell subject to a suspensive condition.
rows.ruling: The Court found a perfected sale because the parties had agreed on the object and price; obtaining the title concerned the sellers' ability to perform, not the birth of the obligation. The later transfer could not defeat the first buyer's enforceable right.
rows.controlling_doctrine: In a contract of sale, ownership is reserved only as security pending full payment, while in a contract to sell the seller's obligation to convey does not arise until the suspensive condition occurs; labels do not control over the parties' stipulations.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed and the judgment ordering specific performance affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard authority for sale versus contract-to-sell classification, perfection, conditions, double sales, and specific performance.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Find consent on object and price, identify whether the event conditions the contract or merely performance, then determine breach, buyer remedies, and any competing purchaser's rights.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Obligations and Contracts - resolution for substantial breach under Article 1191
rows.case_title: Universal Food Corporation v. Court of Appeals, Magdalo V. Francisco, Sr., and Victoriano N. Francisco
rows.short_title: Universal Food v. Court of Appeals
rows.facts_digest: An inventor assigned rights to the Mafran sauce formula and mark in exchange for corporate undertakings, including employment and support for production. The corporation materially failed to perform its reciprocal obligations, prompting an action for rescission.
rows.issue: Whether the corporation's nonperformance was sufficiently substantial to justify resolution of the reciprocal contract.
rows.ruling: The Court sustained resolution because the breached undertakings were fundamental to the consideration and defeated the object of the parties. Article 1191 does not permit resolution for slight or casual violations.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Resolution of reciprocal obligations requires a substantial and fundamental breach that defeats the object of the parties, not a minor, incidental, or casual failure.
rows.disposition: Rescission of the assignment and restoration of the trademark and formula rights were affirmed, with monetary relief as modified.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is a leading Article 1191 authority for substantial breach, reciprocal obligations, rescission, and mutual restitution.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify reciprocal prestations, measure the breach against the contract's principal object, reject resolution for slight breach, and state restitution and damages consequences.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Human Relations and Damages - bad faith in contractual performance
rows.case_title: Air France v. Rafael Carrascoso and Court of Appeals
rows.facts_digest: Carrascoso held a confirmed first-class ticket but was compelled during the trip to surrender his seat to another passenger and move to tourist class. The airline's treatment was humiliating and unsupported by a legitimate contractual justification.
rows.issue: Whether a contractual breach attended by humiliating and bad-faith conduct could support moral and exemplary damages.
rows.ruling: The Court held the airline liable because the breach was carried out fraudulently and in bad faith, offending the passenger's dignity. The Civil Code's human-relations provisions supplied an independent normative basis alongside the contract.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Moral damages may be recovered for breach of contract when the defendant acts fraudulently or in bad faith; Articles 19, 20, and 21 require rights to be exercised with justice, honesty, and good faith.
rows.disposition: Judgment holding the airline liable for compensatory, moral, and exemplary damages substantially affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the classic bridge among contract, abuse of rights, bad faith, and moral and exemplary damages.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Establish the contractual duty and breach, identify conduct showing bad faith or abuse beyond mere nonperformance, and connect each requested class of damages to its statutory basis.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Damages - legal interest before and after finality of judgment
rows.case_title: Dario Nacar v. Gallery Frames and/or Felipe Bordey, Jr.
rows.facts_digest: After an illegal-dismissal judgment became final, the parties disputed the correct computation of backwages, separation pay, and interest over the long enforcement period, especially after the Monetary Board reduced the legal interest rate.
rows.issue: What legal interest rates and accrual rules apply to loans, breached obligations, damages, and final judgments.
rows.ruling: The Court restated the Eastern Shipping framework and adjusted the legal rate to six percent per annum beginning July 1, 2013. Once a monetary judgment becomes final, the total adjudged amount generally earns six percent until satisfaction.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Legal interest depends on the source and stage of the obligation; from finality until full payment, the entire monetary award generally earns six percent per annum under the current BSP rate adopted by the Court.
rows.disposition: Petition partly granted and the monetary award recomputed under the clarified interest rules.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the required authority for virtually every damages or judgment problem involving legal interest.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Build a timeline, classify the obligation, select the rate applicable to each period, identify finality, and compute post-judgment interest on the total award.

rows.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
rows.syllabus_topic: Land Titles and Deeds - mirror doctrine and purchaser in good faith
rows.case_title: Florencia H. Duenas and Daphne Duenas-Montefalcon v. Metropolitan Bank and Trust Company, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Land titles passed through fraudulent transfers and were later acquired and registered by a bank and a realty company despite circumstances indicating adverse claims and defects. The original owners sought recovery of their shares.
rows.issue: When a purchaser of registered land may rely on the face of a Torrens title and when suspicious circumstances defeat good faith.
rows.ruling: The Court held that good faith must exist from acquisition through registration. The mirror doctrine does not protect a buyer with actual knowledge of defects or facts that would prompt a prudent inquiry, and banks are held to heightened diligence.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A purchaser may generally rely on a clean title, but not when red flags, known defects, adverse possession, or the buyer's institutional character demand further inquiry; good faith must persist until registration.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; affected titles were nullified to the extent of petitioners' sixty-percent share, recovery and possession were ordered, and temperate damages awarded.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is a modern En Banc synthesis of the mirror doctrine, innocent purchaser status, forged roots of title, registration, and bank diligence.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Start with the clean-title rule, list all red flags known before registration, apply ordinary or heightened diligence, and determine whether the buyer can retain title against the true owner.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Basic Principles - administrative due process in labor adjudication
rows.case_title: Ang Tibay, represented by Toribio Teodoro, et al. v. Court of Industrial Relations, et al.
rows.facts_digest: A labor dispute reached the Court of Industrial Relations, which relied on material not adequately disclosed or tested by the affected union. On reconsideration, the Supreme Court examined the procedural minimum owed in administrative adjudication.
rows.issue: What fundamental procedural safeguards an administrative or quasi-judicial labor tribunal must observe despite freedom from strict technical rules of evidence.
rows.ruling: The Court articulated the cardinal primary rights of administrative due process, including a real hearing, consideration of evidence presented, a decision supported by substantial evidence, disclosure of the basis of decision, and independent judgment by the tribunal.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Administrative flexibility does not eliminate due process; quasi-judicial findings must rest on substantial evidence disclosed to the parties and independently considered by the decision-maker.
rows.disposition: New trial granted and the case remanded to reopen proceedings under the stated due-process requirements.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the universal anchor for administrative due process and substantial evidence, including labor-agency proceedings.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Enumerate the relevant cardinal rights, identify the missing opportunity or undisclosed evidence, test substantial-evidence support, and state the proper remand or nullification remedy.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Kinds of Employment - fixed-term employment
rows.case_title: Brent School, Inc. and Rev. Gabriel Dimache v. Ronaldo Zamora, et al.
rows.facts_digest: A school administrator knowingly signed successive employment contracts with definite expiration dates and later claimed regular status and illegal dismissal when the final agreed term expired.
rows.issue: Whether the Labor Code categorically prohibits fixed-period employment and whether the agreed term was valid.
rows.ruling: The Court recognized valid fixed-term employment when the period was knowingly and voluntarily agreed upon without force, duress, improper pressure, or circumstances showing that the term was imposed to circumvent security of tenure.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A fixed term is valid only when freely and knowingly stipulated by parties dealing on reasonably equal terms and not used as a device to evade regularization or security-of-tenure protections.
rows.disposition: Government decision reversed; employment was held lawfully terminated upon expiration of the agreed term.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the baseline for testing whether a fixed term is genuine or a prohibited circumvention of regular employment.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Examine voluntariness, bargaining position, recurring renewals, nature of work, and circumvention indicators before treating expiration as a valid cause of separation.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Overseas and Foreign Employment - choice of law and security of tenure
rows.case_title: Pakistan International Airlines Corporation v. Hon. Blas F. Ople, et al.
rows.facts_digest: PIA hired Filipino flight attendants through contracts executed in Manila that specified a fixed period, foreign-law terms, and broad termination authority. It dismissed them before term and invoked the contract's foreign elements.
rows.issue: Whether the foreign carrier could use contractual choice-of-law and termination clauses to defeat mandatory Philippine labor protections.
rows.ruling: The Court applied Philippine labor law because the contracts were made and substantially performed through Philippine employment relations. Private stipulations and foreign-law clauses could not waive security of tenure or authorize dismissal without valid cause.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Mandatory Philippine labor standards and public policy cannot be contracted away through a foreign-law clause when the employment relationship has substantial Philippine contacts.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed; reinstatement or separation pay and backwages relief was sustained as modified.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the anchor for overseas-employment conflicts, public-policy limitations on party autonomy, and illegal dismissal by a foreign employer.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify contract formation, place of work, parties, and mandatory statutes; test the foreign-law clause against public policy and then apply just-cause and due-process requirements.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Employer-Employee Relationship - four-fold test and control of highly skilled talent
rows.case_title: Jose Y. Sonza v. ABS-CBN Broadcasting Corporation
rows.facts_digest: A prominent broadcaster supplied exclusive hosting services through his management corporation under a high-value negotiated agreement. After the relationship ended, he claimed employee status and labor benefits.
rows.issue: Whether the broadcaster was an employee under the four-fold test or an independent contractor engaged for unique talent and results.
rows.ruling: The Court found no employer-employee relationship. ABS-CBN selected programs and standards but did not control the means and methods by which the broadcaster exercised his unique skill, and the agreement reflected independent bargaining through a management company.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Control over the desired result, program standards, or broadcast schedule does not by itself establish employment; the decisive inquiry is control over the means and methods of performing the work, considered with the full four-fold test.
rows.disposition: Petition denied and dismissal for lack of labor jurisdiction affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the leading four-fold-test case for talents, professionals, and high-skill independent contractors.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Apply selection, payment, dismissal power, and especially means-and-methods control; distinguish quality standards from operational control and address the worker's business independence.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Employer-Employee Relationship - control plus economic-reality test
rows.case_title: Angelina Francisco v. National Labor Relations Commission, Kasei Corporation, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Francisco worked for Kasei for years in accounting, liaison, and managerial functions but was labeled a consultant and corporate secretary and omitted from formal payroll records. Her compensation was reduced and later stopped.
rows.issue: Whether she was an employee despite corporate labels and incomplete records, and whether the pay reduction and cessation constituted constructive dismissal.
rows.ruling: The Court used both control and the economic realities of the relationship, finding that her integrated, continuous work and economic dependence established employment. The unilateral reduction and nonpayment of salary amounted to constructive dismissal.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Where the control test alone does not capture a complex relationship, courts may examine total economic reality, particularly whether the worker is economically dependent on the putative employer for continued work in that line of business.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; the NLRC ruling recognizing employment and illegal dismissal was reinstated, with recomputation ordered.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It expands employer-employee analysis beyond labels and is frequently used for consultants, platform work, and disguised employment.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Apply the four-fold test, then evaluate integration, investment, opportunity for profit or loss, permanence, skill, and economic dependence; connect any adverse change to constructive-dismissal doctrine.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Probationary Employment - communicated standards and termination procedure
rows.case_title: Abbott Laboratories, Philippines, et al. v. Pearlie Ann F. Alcaraz
rows.facts_digest: Abbott hired Alcaraz as a probationary employee, gave her written duties and performance expectations, and later terminated her for failing to meet standards. The company, however, did not fully follow an additional internal review procedure.
rows.issue: Whether reasonable standards were communicated at engagement, whether the termination was valid, and what consequence followed from breach of the employer's own procedure.
rows.ruling: The Court found the probationary standards sufficiently communicated and the termination substantively valid. Probationary termination requires reasonable notice rather than the ordinary two-notice just-cause process, but Abbott owed nominal damages for violating its self-imposed procedure.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A probationary employee may be terminated for failure to meet reasonable standards made known at engagement; the employer must give written notice within a reasonable time and may incur nominal damages for breaching a binding internal process.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; the labor arbiter's validity finding was reinstated, modified by a PHP 30,000 nominal-damages award.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the principal case for probationary standards, notice, and the difference between statutory and company-created procedure.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the probationary period, prove standards were reasonably communicated on hiring, connect documented performance to those standards, then assess statutory notice and any separate company process.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Termination - just cause, procedural due process, and nominal damages
rows.case_title: Jenny M. Agabon and Virgilio C. Agabon v. National Labor Relations Commission, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Workers were dismissed for abandonment, a just cause established on the evidence, but the employer failed to provide the notices and hearing opportunity required by labor law.
rows.issue: Whether failure to observe procedural due process makes an otherwise substantively valid just-cause dismissal illegal.
rows.ruling: The Court held that just cause keeps the dismissal valid, but violation of the employee's statutory due-process right warrants nominal damages. It fixed PHP 30,000 for the procedural breach in that just-cause setting.
rows.controlling_doctrine: A dismissal supported by just cause is not invalidated solely by defective procedure; the employer nevertheless incurs nominal damages for violating the employee's statutory right to notice and opportunity to be heard.
rows.disposition: Petition denied; the valid dismissal finding was affirmed with an additional PHP 30,000 nominal-damages award to each employee.
rows.why_bar_relevant: The Agabon doctrine is indispensable to separating substantive cause from procedural compliance and remedies.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Analyze cause and process in separate paragraphs, determine whether the twin-notice requirements were met, uphold or invalidate dismissal on cause, and award the correct nominal damages for the procedural breach.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Remedies - judicial review of NLRC decisions
rows.case_title: St. Martin Funeral Home v. National Labor Relations Commission and Bienvenido Aricayos
rows.short_title: St. Martin Funeral Home v. NLRC
rows.facts_digest: A funeral home brought a Rule 65 petition directly to the Supreme Court to challenge an NLRC ruling arising from an asserted employment relationship.
rows.issue: Which court has initial jurisdiction over a special civil action challenging an NLRC decision for grave abuse of discretion.
rows.ruling: The Court harmonized the Labor Code and the Judiciary Reorganization Act and held that Rule 65 review of NLRC decisions belongs initially in the Court of Appeals, subject to eventual Supreme Court review under Rule 45.
rows.controlling_doctrine: NLRC judgments are reviewed through a Rule 65 petition in the Court of Appeals, not by direct resort to the Supreme Court; the reviewing court asks whether the NLRC committed grave abuse of discretion.
rows.disposition: Petition and records remanded and forwarded to the Court of Appeals for proper action.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It fixes the remedy, forum, and mode of review for one of the most common labor-procedure questions.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the agency decision, choose Rule 65 rather than appeal, file in the Court of Appeals within the governing period, and frame the error as grave abuse supported by the record.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Labor Relations - duty to bargain collectively and unfair labor practice
rows.case_title: Kiok Loy, doing business as Sweden Ice Cream Plant v. National Labor Relations Commission and Pambansang Kilusan ng Paggawa
rows.facts_digest: After a union was certified as exclusive bargaining agent, the employer repeatedly ignored invitations and failed to submit counterproposals to the union's proposed collective bargaining agreement.
rows.issue: Whether the employer's inaction constituted refusal to bargain and whether the union's reasonable proposal could be imposed.
rows.ruling: The Court sustained the unfair-labor-practice finding. A party cannot frustrate collective bargaining through silence and dilatory nonparticipation; on the record, the reasonable union draft was treated as governing.
rows.controlling_doctrine: The duty to bargain in good faith requires meeting and conferring and responding meaningfully to proposals; persistent refusal to participate or make counterproposals is unfair labor practice.
rows.disposition: Petition dismissed; the unfair-labor-practice ruling and imposition of the reasonable union proposal were left in force.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard case for bad-faith bargaining, refusal to bargain, and the exceptional remedy when one party obstructs negotiations.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Establish majority representation and a bargaining demand, chronicle the employer's responses or silence, distinguish hard bargaining from refusal, and state the ULP and remedial consequences.

rows.subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
rows.syllabus_topic: Management Prerogative and Discrimination - no-spouse rules and bona fide occupational qualification
rows.case_title: Star Paper Corporation, et al. v. Ronaldo D. Simbol, et al.
rows.facts_digest: Employees were required to resign or were dismissed under a company policy barring spouses from working in the same enterprise, without a demonstrated conflict tied to their actual jobs.
rows.issue: Whether the no-spouse policy was a valid management prerogative or unlawful discrimination lacking a bona fide occupational justification.
rows.ruling: The Court held that management prerogative is limited by law, fairness, and employees' constitutional and statutory rights. A marital-status restriction requires a compelling business necessity or bona fide occupational qualification supported by evidence, which was absent.
rows.controlling_doctrine: An employment rule that burdens marriage or discriminates by marital status is invalid unless the employer proves the restriction is reasonably necessary to the business and narrowly tied to a bona fide occupational qualification.
rows.disposition: Court of Appeals decision declaring the dismissals illegal and granting reinstatement, backwages, and related relief affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the principal Philippine authority on no-spouse policies, BFOQ, discriminatory rules, and limits of management prerogative.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the protected interest and discriminatory classification, require evidence of actual business necessity and narrow tailoring, then evaluate dismissal and monetary remedies.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Fundamental Principles - mistake of fact and absence of criminal intent
rows.case_title: The United States v. Ah Chong
rows.facts_digest: Awakened at night by someone forcing open the dark room he shared with another servant, Ah Chong repeatedly called out and warned the intruder. Believing a robber was entering, he struck in self-defense, only to discover that the person was his roommate.
rows.issue: Whether an honest and non-negligent mistake about facts that, if true, would justify self-defense negated criminal liability.
rows.ruling: The Court acquitted Ah Chong because he acted without malice under an honest, reasonable, and faultless mistake of fact. Had the circumstances been as he reasonably believed, his defensive act would have been lawful.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Mistake of fact excuses when the mistake is honest and reasonable, concerns facts, is not produced by negligence or bad faith, and would make the act lawful if the supposed facts were true.
rows.disposition: Conviction reversed; accused acquitted and bail bond exonerated, with costs de oficio.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the canonical Philippine illustration of mistake of fact, mens rea, and putative self-defense.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: State the facts as reasonably perceived by the accused, test honesty and freedom from negligence, ask whether those supposed facts complete a justification, and conclude whether criminal intent is negated.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Justifying and Mitigating Circumstances - fulfillment of duty and mistake caused by negligence
rows.case_title: People of the Philippines v. Antonio Z. Oanis and Alberto Galanta
rows.facts_digest: Police officers searching for an escaped convict entered a room and shot a sleeping man without first verifying his identity. The victim was not the fugitive, and the officers invoked obedience to orders, fulfillment of duty, and mistake of fact.
rows.issue: Whether the officers' error excused the killing or fully justified it as fulfillment of duty.
rows.ruling: The Court rejected complete mistake of fact because the officers acted carelessly and without the reasonable verification the circumstances required. Their duty to arrest did not authorize the needless killing of a sleeping person, although incomplete justification affected the penalty.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Mistake of fact is unavailable when produced by negligence; fulfillment of duty requires both a lawful duty and that the injury caused be a necessary consequence of its due performance.
rows.disposition: Accused held liable for homicide and sentenced under the mitigating treatment stated by the Court, with civil indemnity.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard counterpoint to Ah Chong and a core case on incomplete fulfillment of duty and error in person.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Separate the lawful objective from the manner of execution, test necessity and due care, reject fault-induced mistake, and determine whether incomplete justification mitigates rather than exempts.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Stages of Execution - impossible crimes
rows.case_title: Sulpicio Intod v. Court of Appeals and People of the Philippines
rows.facts_digest: Intod and companions fired into a bedroom intending to kill a woman, but she was in another city and no victim occupied the targeted room. He was convicted of attempted murder.
rows.issue: Whether firing at a location where the intended victim was physically absent constituted attempted murder or an impossible crime.
rows.ruling: The Court held that factual or physical impossibility prevented the intended offense against persons from being accomplished. Because the acts would otherwise be criminal and demonstrated dangerousness, liability was for an impossible crime rather than attempted murder.
rows.controlling_doctrine: An impossible crime exists when the offender performs acts against persons or property with evil intent, no other offense is produced, and accomplishment is inherently impossible or the means are inadequate or ineffectual.
rows.disposition: Petition granted; attempted-murder conviction modified to an impossible crime with six months of arresto mayor.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the controlling local application of factual impossibility and distinguishes impossible crimes from attempts.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify criminal intent and overt acts, determine why completion was impossible, exclude another offense actually produced, and select Article 4(2) and Article 59 rather than the attempted stage.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Stages of Execution - attempted and consummated rape
rows.case_title: People of the Philippines v. Ceilito Orita alias Lito
rows.facts_digest: The accused attacked and sexually assaulted the complainant. The trial court characterized the offense as frustrated rape, creating the doctrinal question whether that intermediate stage exists.
rows.issue: Whether rape admits a frustrated stage and what act marks consummation.
rows.ruling: The Court held there is no frustrated rape. Under the doctrine then applied, the slightest penile penetration consummated the offense; before penetration, liability may be attempted rape if overt acts and intent are sufficiently established.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Rape has attempted and consummated stages but no frustrated stage because the act that begins the legally required penetration also completes the offense.
rows.disposition: Trial court judgment modified; accused convicted of consummated rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua with civil indemnity.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard stages-of-execution authority for rape, though current statutory elements and age thresholds must be applied.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Use the current rape statute first, identify overt acts and legally sufficient penetration, rule out a frustrated stage, and then apply the current penalty and civil-liability rules.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Crimes Against Property - consummation of theft
rows.case_title: Aristotel Valenzuela y Natividad v. People of the Philippines and Court of Appeals
rows.facts_digest: Valenzuela took merchandise from a store and passed the checkout area without paying but was apprehended before he could leave the premises with the goods. He argued that the offense was only frustrated theft.
rows.issue: Whether theft is consummated only after the offender gains an opportunity to dispose of the property or whether unlawful taking completes it.
rows.ruling: The Court rejected the supposed frustrated stage. Theft is consummated upon unlawful taking with intent to gain and without the owner's consent; the offender's later ability to freely dispose of the property is not an additional statutory element.
rows.controlling_doctrine: There is no frustrated theft under the Revised Penal Code because completion occurs once all elements, especially unlawful taking, concur; post-taking control or disposal concerns events after consummation.
rows.disposition: Petition denied; conviction for consummated theft affirmed.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the leading authority on theft's stages and statutory-element analysis.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Enumerate theft's elements, locate the moment of unlawful taking, avoid adding the nonstatutory free-disposal test, and conclude whether attempt or consummation applies.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Political Crimes - rebellion and absorption of common crimes
rows.case_title: In the Matter of the Petition for Habeas Corpus of Juan Ponce Enrile, with companion case
rows.facts_digest: Enrile and the Panlilio spouses were charged in connection with an alleged coup attempt under informations that treated rebellion together with murder and other offenses. They invoked the Hernandez doctrine and sought release or bail.
rows.issue: Whether common crimes alleged as necessary means or acts in furtherance of rebellion could be complexed with rebellion.
rows.ruling: The Court reaffirmed that rebellion absorbs acts such as killings and property offenses committed as ingredients or in furtherance of the political offense. The informations therefore charged simple rebellion, a bailable offense under the applicable penalty.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Common crimes committed in furtherance of rebellion and as necessary incidents of the political objective are absorbed in simple rebellion rather than complexed under Article 48, absent an independent criminal purpose.
rows.disposition: Informations read as charging simple rebellion; cases remanded for the trial judge to fix bail as a matter of right.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the modern, accessible reaffirmation of the Hernandez political-offense doctrine and its procedural consequences.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Identify the political objective, test whether each common crime furthered that objective or had an independent purpose, classify the charge, and derive the applicable penalty and bail consequence.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Justifying and Mitigating Circumstances - self-defense and battered woman syndrome
rows.case_title: People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa
rows.facts_digest: After years of severe spousal abuse, Genosa killed her husband during a violent episode and invoked battered woman syndrome as self-defense. Expert evidence described the cumulative psychological effects of the abuse.
rows.issue: Whether battered woman syndrome established complete self-defense despite the absence of unlawful aggression at the moment of the killing.
rows.ruling: The Court recognized battered woman syndrome as relevant evidence but did not acquit because unlawful aggression, an indispensable element of self-defense under the then-applicable framework, was absent at the fatal moment. The syndrome and provocation supported mitigating circumstances.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Self-defense ordinarily requires unlawful aggression; battered woman syndrome may explain perception and diminished self-control and may support statutory defenses or mitigation, but its application must track the governing statute and proven cycle of violence.
rows.disposition: Parricide conviction affirmed but penalty reduced for two mitigating circumstances, allowing parole consideration.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the foundational BWS case and must be read with the later statutory defense in R.A. No. 9262.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Apply the current R.A. No. 9262 BWS provision where available; otherwise analyze unlawful aggression and the remaining self-defense elements, then consider mitigation supported by expert and factual evidence.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto - standardized damages in crimes
rows.case_title: People of the Philippines v. Ireneo Jugueta
rows.facts_digest: Jugueta fired at a family inside their dwelling, killing two children and wounding other occupants. On appeal, the Court addressed both criminal liability and inconsistent awards of civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages across serious crimes.
rows.issue: What standardized civil-damages framework should courts apply according to the crime, penalty, qualifying circumstances, and stage of execution.
rows.ruling: The Court affirmed the convictions with modifications and supplied a structured schedule for civil indemnity and moral and exemplary damages. The amounts depend on the imposable penalty, attendance of qualifying or aggravating circumstances, and whether the offense was consummated, frustrated, or attempted.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Civil indemnity follows from the fact of death or qualifying offense without separate proof, moral damages may likewise be presumed in specified crimes, and exemplary damages depend on qualifying or aggravating circumstances; current amounts must follow the latest controlling cases.
rows.disposition: Appeal dismissed; convictions affirmed with modified penalties and standardized monetary awards.
rows.why_bar_relevant: It is the standard damages table for criminal-law answers and sentencing analysis.
rows.how_to_use_in_alac: Determine the exact crime, stage, penalty, and circumstances first; then apply the latest Jugueta-line amounts separately for civil indemnity, moral, exemplary, temperate, and actual damages.

rows.subject: Criminal Law
rows.syllabus_topic: Special Penal Laws - plunder, vagueness, and pattern of overt criminal acts
rows.case_title: Joseph Ejercito Estrada v. Sandiganbayan and People of the Philippines
rows.facts_digest: Former President Estrada challenged his prosecution under the Plunder Law, asserting that the statute's concepts of combination, series, and pattern of overt or criminal acts were vague and denied due process.
rows.issue: Whether R.A. No. 7080 adequately defines plunder and the prosecution's burden to prove a pattern of predicate acts.
rows.ruling: The Court upheld the statute. Read as a whole and with ordinary legal meaning, it gives fair notice and requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the elements, including a combination or series showing an overall unlawful scheme and the statutory aggregate amount.
